title: TikTok and Its Role in COVID-19 Information Propagation (Letter to the editor, Journal of Adolescent Health)
screen_reason: A research letter, but it reports an original quantitative content analysis with a denominator: the 100 most popular videos in each of the three largest COVID-19 hashtags on TikTok ('covid-19', 'covid19', 'coronavirus') as of 12 July 2020 were categorised, and 0.66% were found to provide 'misleading or inaccurate health advice' — a CONTENT share of items. Included despite the letter format because the number is an original finding, not commentary; the near-total absence of method detail is recorded as low confidence.

estimates.country: Not stated for the video sample (the letter's framing concerns U.S. adolescents; the hashtags themselves are global)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most popular COVID-19 hashtag videos on TikTok that provided misleading or inaccurate health advice
estimates.value_raw: .66% provided misleading or inaccurate health advice (of the 100 most popular videos in each of three hashtags, i.e. 300 videos; 2/300 = 0.67%)
estimates.denominator: The 100 most popular videos in each of the three largest COVID-19-related TikTok hashtags ('covid-19', 'covid19', 'coronavirus') as of 12 July 2020, i.e. 300 videos; TikTok search results are sorted by likes received per post
estimates.definition: Video categorised as providing misleading or inaccurate health advice, as opposed to pragmatic health information, a health-care professional's video, a patient recovery video, or a satirical depiction of everyday quarantine activities. No coding rule, coder count, or ground-truth reference is given.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Given social media's ability to propagate factually inaccurate medical information at an alarming rate [6], we analyzed the 100 most popular videos in each of the three largest COVID-19-related categories on TikTok." — the letter offers no operational definition beyond the label "misleading or inaccurate health advice".
estimates.source_quote: Our findings revealed that, on average, 6.33% of videos were filmed by health care professionals, and 2.66% were filmed by young adult patients tracking their recovery journeys. In addition, 15.66% of videos communicated pragmatic health information, and .66% provided misleading or inaccurate health advice, with the remaining videos depicting everyday quarantine activities in a satirical manner.
estimates.page_loc: Letter to the editor, J Adolesc Health 67 (2020) 730, single page
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Coding by the two authors (premedicine students, Eberly College of Science, Penn State) is implied but never described: no codebook, no number of coders, no interrater reliability, no external reference standard, and no statement of who judged accuracy. This is the study's principal weakness.
estimates.moderator_quote: Videos are sorted into hashtags, with search results directly sorted by likes received per post. ... we analyzed the 100 most popular videos in each of the three largest COVID-19-related categories on TikTok. As of July 12, 2020, these were videos earmarked with the hashtags "covid-19," "covid19," and "coronavirus".
estimates.notes: denom_selection = curated and denom_scope = topical: a popularity-truncated top-100 set per hashtag, not a random or full sample, so the estimate speaks to the most-liked COVID-19 TikTok content only. The reported percentages are all exact x/300 (19/300 = 6.33%, 8/300 = 2.67%, 47/300 = 15.67%, 2/300 = 0.67%), which confirms a pooled 300-video denominator despite the wording 'on average'; the numerator is therefore about 2 videos, so the estimate is extremely imprecise. The four named categories sum to 25.3%, with the remaining ~75% described as satirical depictions of everyday quarantine activities — a category that was evidently not assessed for accuracy, so videos with misleading content could sit unexamined inside it. confidence = low: no coding procedure, no definition, no reliability, no country, and a two-item numerator. quote_verbatim = false: the extracted PDF text of this two-column letter interleaves the two columns line by line, so the sentence carrying the value is not a contiguous span anywhere in the text file. The longest contiguous verbatim fragment containing the value is 'formation, and .66% provided misleading or inaccurate health'; the source_quote above is that sentence reassembled in reading order, with no words added or altered.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) No breakdown by hashtag is given, so the three hashtag sub-samples cannot be split into separate rows (the pooled 0.66% is the only stated share and 'on average' is not explained). 2) The other content categories (6.33% health-care professionals, 2.66% patient recovery journeys, 15.66% pragmatic health information, remainder satirical) are not misinformation shares and were not extracted. 3) Hashtag view totals (4.4 billion, 33.3 billion, 93.1 billion views) are platform reach figures with no misinformation numerator, so they support no EXPOSURE or REACH row; the letter also gives no engagement share for the misleading videos, only the unquantified remark that health-professional videos 'were often among the most widely liked and shared', so no SHARING or CONCENTRATION row is possible. 4) The 45.6 million U.S. active users and 63.5% aged under 29 are cited from Statista, i.e. from elsewhere, and excluded under R8. 5) It is unclear whether the ~75% 'satirical' remainder was screened for accuracy at all; if it was not, 0.66% is a lower bound on misleading content in the sample. An adjudicator may reasonably prefer to drop this study on method-reporting grounds — the value is verbatim and has a denominator, so it passes the letter of the criteria, but nothing about the coding is reproducible.

rob.design: Single-page letter to the editor reporting a cross-sectional content analysis. Sample: the 100 most popular videos in each of the three largest COVID-19-related TikTok hashtags ('covid-19', 'covid19', 'coronavirus'), retrieved as of 12 July 2020, with TikTok search results ordered by likes per post (n = 300 implied). Videos were assigned to categories (health-care professional creator, patient recovery journey, pragmatic health information, misleading or inaccurate health advice, satirical quarantine content). No codebook, coder count, coder qualification, training, blinding, reliability statistic, or accuracy reference standard is reported; no sampling frame beyond the hashtag popularity ranking; no country restriction stated; no statistical analysis. Authors are two premedicine undergraduates. Reporting is far below systematic-review standards for a content analysis.
